title: Genetics and Evolution
seo_title: Year 11 Science: Genetics and Evolution Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_code: KS4 Biology: Inheritance, variation and evolution
standard_text: Sexual and asexual reproduction; meiosis; DNA and the genome; genetic inheritance, including Punnett squares; inherited disorders; sex determination; variation; evolution by natural selection; selective breeding and genetic engineering; evidence for evolution, including fossils and antibiotic resistance; classification of living organisms.
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on inheritance and evolution: meiosis, Punnett squares, cystic fibrosis, sex determination, natural selection, antibiotic resistance and classification. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Each parent gives one allele of every gene.
key_sub: Use a Punnett square to find the chances.
body_html:
How to think about it

Meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosomes.

  • Dominant alleles show with one copy; recessive alleles need two copies.
  • A carrier has one recessive allele but not the disorder.
  • Natural selection: variation → the best adapted survive and reproduce → their alleles become more common.
Example

Ff × Ff. Chance of cystic fibrosis?

FF, Ff, Ff, ff

1 out of 4

Answer: 25%

Example

Scientific name Panthera leo. Genus?

Genus first

Answer: Panthera

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a carrier has the disorder.
  • Thinking bacteria get used to antibiotics.
  • Thinking gametes have 46 chromosomes.

faq.q: How do you work out the chance of an inherited disorder?
faq.a: Draw a Punnett square with each parent's alleles. Count the boxes with the genotype you want out of 4.
Someone with one recessive allele for a disorder. They do not have the disorder but can pass the allele on.

faq.q: How does antibiotic resistance show evolution?
faq.a: A mutation makes some bacteria resistant. When an antibiotic is used, these survive and reproduce, so resistant bacteria become common.

items.q: Isla's sample has 5,000 bacteria. 1% of them have a resistance gene. An antibiotic kills all the others. How many bacteria are left?
1,000 bacteria are in a culture, and 2% are resistant. An antibiotic kills every non-resistant cell. How many are killed (Amelia's lab)?
A farmer sprays the same insecticide for years. It kills fewer insects each year. A student says: “Each insect got used to the spray.” What is wrong with this claim?
c: Evolution is too slow to see.
Individuals do not change their genes to meet a need; selection acts on existing variation.
items.e: That is Lamarck's idea, not natural selection.

c: All individuals changed in the same way during their lives.
Dark moths were hidden from birds, so they survived and reproduced more.
The environment does not affect which individuals survive.
The moths turned dark because they needed to hide.
items.e: Natural selection acts on traits that are already present and inherited.

items.q: Mice with fur that matches the ground have more pups that survive. Which factor of natural selection does this show?
c: better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce more
items.e: The four factors: overproduction, variation, competition and differential survival.

items.q: Why should patients finish a course of antibiotics?

to kill all the bacteria so none survive to become resistant

items.q: What is genetic engineering?
